howToMeasure.text: Rest quietly for at least 5 minutes before checking. Place your index and middle fingers on the inside of your wrist below the thumb, and count the beats for 60 seconds while seated.
howToMeasure.source: American Heart Association: All About Heart Rate (Pulse)

whyItMatters.text: A typical resting heart rate for adults ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute. Highly trained athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 beats per minute.
whyItMatters.source: American Heart Association: All About Heart Rate (Pulse)

hazardEffects.text: In microgravity, fluid shifts toward the head and blood plasma volume decreases, altering cardiovascular regulation and impacting stability when standing in gravity.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Roadmap: Risk of Orthostatic Intolerance

selfCare.text: Rest seated quietly for 5 to 10 minutes and repeat the measurement to verify the reading.
Check your daily fluid intake and consider electrolyte replacement after exercise sessions.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if resting heart rate is consistently above 100 bpm, drops below 40 bpm (or below known athletic baseline), or occurs alongside chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness.

howToMeasure.text: Position the forehead Double Sensor heat-flux device securely against the skin during pre-exercise rest. Avoid taking measurements immediately after intense physical activity.

whyItMatters.text: Body temperature measures the body's ability to generate and dissipate heat. Typical resting temperature in adults averages around 37°C (98.6°F) and fluctuates across the daily cycle.

hazardEffects.text: Resting core body temperature in astronauts gradually increases by approximately 1°C over the first 75 mission days in microgravity; authors note a possible correlation with impaired convective heat dissipation and systemic inflammatory markers rather than established causation.

selfCare.text: Rest in an area with active cabin ventilation and airflow to promote convective cooling.
Drink water and repeat the temperature measurement after 20 to 30 minutes of inactive rest.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if core temperature exceeds 38.5°C (101.3°F), does not return toward baseline after resting, or is accompanied by chills or acute malaise.

howToMeasure.text: Rest seated quietly for 5 minutes with feet flat and arm supported at heart level before taking a cuff measurement. Avoid talking during cuff inflation.
howToMeasure.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings

whyItMatters.text: Blood pressure reflects how hard the heart must work to pump blood through the body. A typical resting terrestrial reading is systolic below 120 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg.
whyItMatters.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings

hazardEffects.text: In microgravity, fluid shifts toward the head and systemic blood vessels widen (vasodilatation), lowering vascular resistance. In a study of 8 male ISS astronauts between flight days 85 and 192, 24-hour average blood pressure fell by 8 mmHg systolic and 9 mmHg diastolic.
hazardEffects.source: Norsk et al. 2015, Journal of Physiology

selfCare.text: If a spot measurement is unusually high or low, remain quietly seated for 5 minutes and repeat the measurement on the same arm.
Keep up with daily hydration, as low blood volume can lead to lightheadedness or feeling faint when standing.
selfCare.source: NASA Human Research Roadmap: Risk of Orthostatic Intolerance

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if blood pressure is unusually low with dizziness or feeling faint, if systolic exceeds 180 mmHg or diastolic exceeds 120 mmHg, or if reading is accompanied by vision changes, acute headache, or chest pain.
whenToEscalate.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings

howToMeasure.text: Clean the puncture site, dry thoroughly, and apply a fresh capillary blood sample to an approved glucometer test strip, noting whether the test is fasting or post-meal.

whyItMatters.text: Blood glucose reflects how the body manages carbohydrates. In fasting adults, typical levels sit between 70 and 99 mg/dL, and below 140 mg/dL two hours after a meal.

hazardEffects.text: Reduced muscle activity in microgravity, combined with physical confinement, can lower insulin sensitivity and change how the body processes glucose after eating.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes from Altered Nutrition

selfCare.text: If a reading is unexpectedly low, re-measure and notify the Crew Medical Officer.
Log meals and follow planned exercise sessions to help the body use insulin well.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if blood glucose drops below 54 mg/dL or exceeds 250 mg/dL, or if accompanied by nausea, shakiness, confusion, or weakness.

howToMeasure.text: Log total hours slept over the previous 24-hour crew duty cycle, including any restorative naps.

whyItMatters.text: Adequate sleep is critical for alertness, decision making, and immune defense. Adults typically require 7 or more hours per night.

hazardEffects.text: Disrupted circadian rhythms, absence of natural daylight, background cabin noise, and sleeping in microgravity frequently lead to fragmented sleep and accumulated sleep debt.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Performance Decrements from Sleep Loss

selfCare.text: Set up your sleep quarters for rest: ensure earplugs are fitted, use an eye mask, and confirm cabin ventilation is flowing properly.
Limit screen time and bright light exposure in the 60 minutes before scheduled sleep.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if sleep is less than 4 hours on two or more consecutive duty cycles, or if daytime drowsiness impairs critical operational mission tasks.

howToMeasure.text: Select a rating from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good) reflecting your mood and operational stress over the last 24 hours.

whyItMatters.text: Self-reported mood helps track emotional resilience, stress, and crew dynamics during long, isolated mission phases.

hazardEffects.text: Living in confined quarters far from Earth, with heavy workloads and sensory monotony, can contribute to fatigue, low energy, and interpersonal stress.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Adverse Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders

selfCare.text: Set aside time for relaxation, listen to music, read, or connect with family and friends on Earth through private messaging.
Talk openly with crewmates about workload adjustments if fatigue is building up.

whenToEscalate.text: Reach out to the Crew Medical Officer or flight psychologist if sustained low mood, anxiety, or lack of motivation begins impacting daily mission tasks.
